item: Other randomised trials of AI coding tools and their designs
citation: Peng, S., Kalliamvakou, E., Cihon, P., Demirer, M. 'The Impact of AI on Developer Productivity: Evidence from GitHub Copilot'. arXiv:2302.06590v1, 13 Feb 2023 (single version). https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.06590

Cui, K. Z., Demirer, M., Jaffe, S., Musolff, L., Peng, S., Salz, T. 'The Effects of Generative AI on High-Skilled Work: Evidence from Three Field Experiments with Software Developers'. Working paper draft dated February 2025, https://economics.mit.edu/sites/default/files/inline-files/draft_copilot_experiments.pdf ; published online in Management Science 27 Feb 2026, DOI 10.1287/mnsc.2025.00535 (date and abstract from the Crossref record, https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1287/mnsc.2025.00535).

Paradis, E., Grey, K., Madison, Q., Nam, D., Macvean, A., Meimand, V., Zhang, N., Ferrari-Church, B., Chandra, S. 'How much does AI impact development speed? An enterprise-based randomized controlled trial'. arXiv:2410.12944v3, 11 Nov 2024 (v1 16 Oct 2024). https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.12944 . [uncertain] Reported as published in ICSE-SEIP 2025, pp. 618-629, but only seen in another paper's reference list.

METR. 'We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design'. Blog post, 24 Feb 2026. https://metr.org/blog/2026-02-24-uplift-update/ (the one 2026 report of a randomised productivity trial found; covered in depth by a separate item).

Shen, J. H., Tamkin, A. 'How AI Impacts Skill Formation'. arXiv:2601.20245v2, 1 Feb 2026 (paper dated 3 Feb 2026). https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.20245 (2026 randomised experiment, outcome is learning rather than productivity).

Murphy-Hill, E., Butler, J., Savelieva, A. 'Adoption and Impact of Command-Line AI Coding Agents: A Study of Microsoft's Early 2026 Rollout of Claude Code and GitHub Copilot CLI'. arXiv:2607.01418v1, 1 Jul 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01418 (NOT randomised; included as the 2026 comparison case).
source_tier: Peng 2023: preprint, never seen in a peer-reviewed venue. Cui et al.: working paper, later peer-reviewed (Management Science, online Feb 2026). Paradis 2024: company research preprint (Google). METR 2026: research-organisation blog post, not a paper. Shen and Tamkin 2026: company research preprint (Anthropic). Murphy-Hill 2026: company research preprint (Microsoft).
access_status: Fully read from the PDF text: Peng 2023 (whole paper), Cui et al. February 2025 MIT draft (main text, not appendices), Paradis v3 (main text). METR post: full page text read. Shen and Tamkin, Murphy-Hill: abstract, design, results and limitations sections read, not every page. NOT opened: the Management Science final text (publisher returned 403; only the Crossref abstract was read), the SSRN page (403), the AEA trial registry entry AEARCTR-0014530 (500 error).
author_credentials: Peng: Microsoft Research (Peng), GitHub (Kalliamvakou, Cihon), MIT Sloan (Demirer). GitHub makes Copilot and Microsoft owns GitHub, so three of four authors work for the vendor. Cui et al.: economists at Princeton, MIT, Wharton, plus Jaffe and Peng at Microsoft; the firms ran the experiments and shared data; Demirer and Salz funded by the MIT GenAI Initiative. Paradis: all nine authors at Google, evaluating Google's own internal tools (they state this risk themselves). METR: non-profit AI evaluation organisation, no product to sell. Shen and Tamkin: Anthropic (Shen via the Anthropic Fellows Program); Anthropic sells an AI coding tool, and the finding cuts against its commercial interest. Murphy-Hill et al.: Microsoft, which the authors note 'sells AI tools, encourages their use, and owns GitHub'.
exact_quotes: Peng, Study Design: 'The experiment began on May 15, 2022 and ended on June 20, 2022, right before GitHub Copilot became generally available.'
Peng, Study Design: 'Once participants signed the contract, they were randomly split into control and treatment groups.'
Peng, Introduction: 'The control group did not have access to GitHub Copilot but was otherwise unconstrained, i.e., they were free to use internet search and Stack Overflow to complete the task.'

Peng, Results: 'Conditioning on completing the task, the average completion time from the treated group is 71.17 minutes and 160.89 minutes for the control group. This represents a 55.8% reduction in completion time. The p-value for the t-test is 0.0017, and a 95% confidence interval for the improvement is between [21%, 89%].'

Peng, Results: 'The 95 developers were randomly assigned into control and treated groups, with 45 in the treated group and 50 in control. Thirty-five developers from both the treated and control groups completed the task and survey.'
Cui, section 2.2 (Microsoft): 'The experiment ended on May 3rd, 2023, as growing awareness of AI-assisted coding tools led the control group participants to seek access to Copilot.'
Cui, footnote 8: 'A small number of developers in the control group nevertheless got access to Copilot because they were working on related tools.'

Cui, Introduction: 'The experiment at Microsoft started before Copilot was widely known (and before the release of ChatGPT), and initial uptake was low. Shortly after a larger fraction of developers in the treatment group started using it, the control group was also allowed access.'

Cui, section 4.1: 'we have to discuss a key complication: our data comes from experiments where the control group was eventually also allowed to access GitHub Copilot. This is not a challenge for identification, but it reduces the power of our instrument if we employ the naive strategy detailed above.'
Cui, footnote 3: 'The exact implementation of these experiments was rather ad-hoc as they were driven by business considerations at these companies rather than research goals.'

Cui, section 2.2: 'Randomization was implemented at both the individual and the team levels. In particular, 616 developers were individually randomized and 1,130 developers were randomized at the team level, with an average team size of 6.2.'
Cui, section 2.2 (Anonymous Company): 'all users gained access to the tool over a period of two months, but access dates were randomized, with some teams gaining access six weeks before others.'
Cui, Introduction: 'These experiments lasted 2 to 8 months after which all groups were granted access to Copilot.'

Paradis, section IV: 'Participants were randomly assigned to either the AI or no-AI condition after they had completed the pre-task questionnaire and reviewed the AI features. The coding task was identical for the AI and no-AI condition, except for the setup steps, which instructed participants to either enable or disable AI features in their IDE, respectively.'
Paradis, section IV: 'these features were all in production and commonly available to all developers across the company before the task, but had varied usage rates.'
Paradis, Abstract: 'Our best estimate of the size of this effect, controlling for factors known to influence developer time on task, stands at about 21%, although our confidence interval is large.'

Paradis, section VI.C: 'our confidence intervals are large, and as a result the estimate is not statistically significant at the p < 0.05 level (estimate of experimental condition on best-fit Model 2, β1 = −0.24; 95%CI = [−0.51, 0.03], p = 0.086, NS).'

Paradis, Abstract: 'we cannot assume that the effect size obtained in our lab study will necessarily apply more broadly, or that the effect of AI found using internal Google tooling in the summer of 2024 will translate across tools and over time.'

METR 2026: 'The primary reason is that we have observed a significant increase in developers choosing not to participate in the study because they do not wish to work without AI, which likely biases downwards our estimate of AI-assisted speedup.'
METR 2026: 'When surveyed, 30% to 50% of developers told us that they were choosing not to submit some tasks because they did not want to do them without AI.'

METR 2026: 'Some developers were less likely to complete tasks that they submitted if they were assigned to the AI-disallowed condition. One developer did not complete any of the tasks that were assigned to the AI-disallowed condition.'

METR 2026: 'An alternative design is to randomize at the developer level instead of the task level, i.e. each participant either uses AI for all their tasks or for none. This alleviates some of the task-level selection problems, however it makes the developer-level selection problems worse, and has lower power in detecting productivity effects.'

Shen and Tamkin, section 5.1 (pilots): 'We tested different mechanisms to ensure participants in the control condition (No AI) did not use AI for the task. However, despite more explicit instructions, around 25% in the control group participants still used AI.'
Murphy-Hill 2026, Threats to Validity: 'In Part 1, adopters self-select, so the synthetic counterfactual may be biased'
key_claims: Peng 2023: in a one-off lab-style task (write an HTTP server in JavaScript), freelancers given Copilot finished 55.8% faster than a control group without it. The authors call it, to their knowledge, the first controlled experiment on AI tool productivity in professional software development.

Cui et al.: across three company-run field experiments with 4,867 developers, using Copilot raised weekly completed pull requests by 26.08% (SE 10.3%). Less experienced developers adopted more and gained more. Each experiment alone is noisy.

Paradis 2024: 96 Google engineers on one enterprise-grade C++ task were about 21% faster with three AI features than with them switched off, but the regression estimate is not significant at the 5% level.

METR Feb 2026: the task-randomised follow-up to its 2025 trial gives 'an unreliable signal' because developers decline to take part, hold back tasks, or fail to complete tasks rather than work without AI. METR is changing the design.
Shen and Tamkin 2026: in a randomised learning experiment, the AI group scored 17% lower on a quiz about a new library, with no statistically significant speed gain in the main study.

Murphy-Hill 2026: Microsoft's own early-2026 study of Claude Code and Copilot CLI does not randomise at all. It estimates a 24% rise in merged pull requests among adopters from a synthetic control built from engineers who never used either tool.
headline_figures: Peng: '55.8% reduction in completion time'. Treated mean 71.17 minutes against control mean 160.89 minutes, conditional on finishing. 95% CI [21%, 89%], p = 0.0017. Comparison group: no Copilot, internet search allowed. Data May to June 2022. My arithmetic check: (160.89 - 71.17) / 160.89 = 55.8%.
Peng: 95 recruited, 45 treated and 50 control. Success rate 7 percentage points higher for treated, not significant (95% CI [-0.11, 0.25]). Participants in both groups guessed a 35% gain.

Cui: '26.08% increase (SE: 10.3%) in completed tasks' (weekly pull requests), pooled precision-weighted IV estimate, 4,867 developers. By firm: Microsoft 27.38% (SE 12.88), Accenture 17.94% (SE 18.72), anonymous company 54.03% (SE 42.63). Only the Microsoft estimate is significant on its own.
Cui: commits +13.55% (SE 10.0%), builds +38.38% (SE 12.55%). Including a second, abandoned Accenture experiment the pull-request figure falls to 21.34% (SE 9.92%).
Cui, Microsoft adoption: 8.5% of the treated group signed up in the first two weeks; 42.5% after reminder emails in February 2023; by January 2024 adoption was 75.6% treated against 64.0% control.

Paradis: AI group 96 minutes (N = 47, SE 9.3) against 114 minutes (N = 46, SE 8.1) for no-AI; t-test on log time p = .038. Regression estimate 'about 21%' (β = -0.24, 95% CI [-0.51, 0.03], p = 0.086); a second model gives 26%. Data June to July 2024.

METR 2026 (sign convention is METR's, negative means less time): returning developers -18% (CI -38% to +9%), new developers -4% (CI -15% to +9%). 57 developers, 143 repos, 800+ tasks. Pay $50 an hour, down from $150. 30% to 50% of developers said they withheld some tasks.
Shen and Tamkin: 17% lower quiz score, 'two grade points' (Cohen's d = 0.738, p = 0.010), main study n = 52.
Murphy-Hill 2026 (observational): '+24.0% lift in PRs/engineer/day' [95% CI +14.5%, +33.7%], post-period 5 January to 29 April 2026.
sample_and_method: PENG 2023. Unit of randomisation: individual developer, between subjects, one fixed task. No-AI control: yes (no Copilot, web search and Stack Overflow allowed). Data: 15 May to 20 June 2022, before Copilot's general release. Sample: 95 Upwork freelancers (45 treated, 50 control), mostly aged 25 to 34, mostly from India and Pakistan. Trouble keeping a control: none reported. The only compliance problem ran the other way: five treated participants never finished Copilot sign-up and started without it.

CUI ET AL., MICROSOFT. Unit: mixed. 616 developers randomised individually, 1,130 by team (average team 6.2). No-AI control: yes, control had no Copilot access. Data: first week of September 2022 to 3 May 2023, with outcomes followed into 2024. Sample: 1,746 developers, 50.4% treated. Trouble keeping a control: yes. The experiment ended because control developers sought access; a few controls got access anyway; 0.5% of controls had adopted early on.

CUI ET AL., ACCENTURE. Unit: individual developer. No-AI control: yes, until December 2023. Data: last week of July 2023 to December 2023, adoption tracked to April 2024. Sample: 320 developers in Southeast Asia, 61.3% treated. Trouble: control given access after about four months; a separate second Accenture experiment was abandoned after a layoff hit 42% of participants.

CUI ET AL., ANONYMOUS FORTUNE 100 FIRM. Unit: team, with randomised access dates (staggered rollout). No lasting no-AI control: everyone got access within about six weeks, so the comparison is early against late. Data: September to October 2023 rollout. Sample: 3,054 developers. Trouble: the design never tried to hold a control group; the authors say differences in treatment status lasted 'only a short time'.

CUI ET AL., METHOD. Company-run rollouts, analysed afterwards (the trial was post-registered). Because many treated developers never used the tool and controls later did, the 26% is an instrumental-variable estimate of the effect on those who used it, weighted towards weeks when treated and control adoption differed most.

PARADIS 2024 (GOOGLE). Unit: individual developer, between subjects, one fixed task of up to about three hours. No-AI control: yes, by instruction. Control participants were told to disable three AI features that were already in production for all staff. Data: recruited June to July 2024. Sample: 96 full-time Google engineers, 48 per arm, 93 completed. Trouble keeping a control: none reported, and the paper does not say whether it checked that control participants kept the features off.

METR FOLLOW-UP (reported Feb 2026). Unit: task, within developer. Developers nominate their own tasks, then each is assigned AI-allowed or AI-disallowed. Data: from August 2025. Sample: 57 open-source developers (10 returning, 47 new). Trouble keeping a control: yes, on three fronts. Developers declined to join, withheld tasks, and were less likely to finish AI-disallowed tasks.

SHEN AND TAMKIN 2026. Unit: individual, between subjects, fixed tasks, about one hour. No-AI control: yes. Sample: 52 crowd-recruited programmers, paid a flat $150. Data-collection dates are not stated in the sections read. Trouble keeping a control: yes, in pilots. 35% of the no-AI group used AI on the first platform and about 25% still did after explicit warnings; the main study moved platforms and used screen recordings to verify compliance.

MURPHY-HILL 2026 (MICROSOFT). Not randomised. Self-selected adopters compared with a synthetic control of never-users. Pre-period 1 October 2024 to 4 January 2026, post-period 5 January to 29 April 2026.
evidence_offered: Peng: timestamps from GitHub Classroom on a test-suite-graded task, one t-test. Cui: GitHub telemetry (pull requests, commits, builds) at developer-week level, two-stage least squares with assignment as the instrument. Paradis: IDE-logged time on task, t-test and linear regressions with self-reported covariates. METR: self-recorded task times under task-level random assignment, plus surveys and interviews with participants about what they held back. Shen and Tamkin: a pre-registered quiz and platform transcripts, with screen recordings. Murphy-Hill: Azure DevOps pull-request counts and a Bayesian structural time-series model.
data_vintage: Peng: data May to June 2022, published Feb 2023, one arXiv version. Cui: data September 2022 to roughly April 2024; SSRN posting September 2024 [uncertain, search snippet only]; draft read here is dated February 2025; Management Science online 27 Feb 2026. Figures quoted are from the February 2025 draft, and the 26.08% (SE 10.3%) matches the published abstract. Paradis: data summer 2024; v3 of 11 Nov 2024 read. METR: data from August 2025, posted 24 Feb 2026. Shen and Tamkin: v2, 1 Feb 2026. Murphy-Hill: data to 29 April 2026, posted 1 Jul 2026. The newest completed randomised productivity estimate with a no-AI control in this set uses 2024 data.
figure_provenance: 55.8%: Peng et al. abstract and Results. It is a reduction in completion time, not a 55.8% rise in output. Later papers restate it loosely: Cui et al. write 'the 58% decrease Peng et al. (2023) find', Paradis et al. write 'a 56% speed increase', Shen and Tamkin write '55.5% faster'. Use 55.8% and call it a cut in time taken.
Peng dates: the text says the experiment 'began on May 15, 2022' but the Figure 1 note says the Upwork job posting started 'May 25th 2022'. The paper does not reconcile these.
Peng completers: 'Thirty-five developers from both the treated and control groups completed the task and survey' is ambiguous (35 in each group, or 35 in total). Do not cite a completion count.

26% / 26.08%: Cui et al., pooled weighted-IV estimate for pull requests. The standard error is 10.3%, so a rough 95% range is about 6% to 46%. 'Tasks' means pull requests. It is the effect on developers who took up the tool, not on everyone offered it. An alternative pooled figure of 21.34% appears when the abandoned second Accenture experiment is included.

Cui abstract wording changed between versions: the February 2025 draft says 'Though each experiment is noisy'; the Management Science abstract says 'Although each experiment is noisy and results vary across experiments'.

Cui internal date inconsistencies: Microsoft 'ended on May 3rd, 2023' in section 2.2 but 'the conclusion of the experiment in April 2023' in section 3; the anonymous firm 'started in October 2023' but invites went out 'between September 2023 and October 2023'.

About 21%: Paradis et al. abstract. It comes from regression Model 2 and is not significant at 5%. The significant result is the unadjusted t-test (96 against 114 minutes, about 16% less time by my arithmetic). The paper's text gives mean log times that look swapped between groups (AI 4.6, no-AI 4.3), which reads as a typo.
METR -18% and -4%: METR's post, where negative means tasks took less time. METR itself says the estimate is unreliable.
population_and_transfer: Peng: low-income freelancers on a greenfield toy task; weak transfer to staff engineers in existing codebases, as Paradis et al. point out. Cui: ordinary employees doing their real jobs at three large firms, the best transfer in the set, but the tool is 2022 to 2023 autocomplete Copilot, not agents. Paradis: Google engineers on Google's internal tools and monorepo; realistic task, single company. METR: experienced open-source maintainers on their own repositories. Shen and Tamkin: crowd-recruited programmers learning an unfamiliar library in an hour. None of the randomised estimates covers agentic tools in ordinary company work.
outcome_measured: Task speed: Peng, Paradis, METR (time to complete). On-the-job output: Cui (weekly pull requests, commits, builds, build success rate), Murphy-Hill (merged pull requests). Immediate quiz score: Shen and Tamkin. None measures employment, postings or delayed retention.
limitations_stated: Peng: 'This study examines a standardized programming task in an experiment to obtain a precise measure of productivity, instead of a task where developers collaborate on large projects'; and 'this study does not examine the effects of AI on code quality.'

Cui: 'While standard errors are consistently large and the effect sizes differ across the three different companies'; low power from 'factors that reduce the take-up and duration of the three experiments'; implementation 'rather ad-hoc'; around 30% to 40% of engineers never tried the tool.

Paradis: 'There may be external validity constraints on our estimates given how participants were all Google employees'; 'We cannot, however, fully eliminate the risk associated with us evaluating our own team's developer tools'; 'a "true estimate" of the contribution of AI tools to developer speed will be a moving target.'

METR: 'our data is only very weak evidence for the size of this increase'; pay cut from $150 to $50 an hour 'also likely contributed to the higher selection'; self-reported time is unreliable for developers running several agents at once.
Shen and Tamkin: one chat-based task over one hour; participants had 'not the same incentive to learn the library as if it were required for their actual job'.
Murphy-Hill: merged PRs are 'an imperfect proxy for throughput'; adopters self-select; one company, one early-2026 window.
counter_evidence: Against a blanket claim that the no-AI control cannot be run: Peng (2022) and Paradis (2024) report no difficulty at all, and Shen and Tamkin ran a clean no-AI arm in 2026 once they used screen recordings. All three are short, fixed-task sessions lasting hours. The trouble shows up where the control must last weeks or months inside real work (Cui's Microsoft arm in 2022 to 2023, METR in 2025 to 2026). Against reading METR's problem as new: Cui's Microsoft control group was already asking for access by spring 2023, so pressure on the control predates agentic tools. Against the headline gains themselves: Paradis's adjusted estimate is not significant, two of Cui's three firm-level estimates are not significant, and Murphy-Hill cites field experiments that found 'no significant change in merged pull requests'.
alternative_explanations: Cui's Microsoft control ended for business reasons as much as developer demand: the firms ran these trials 'to decide whether or how extensively to adopt these technologies', so ending the hold-out once the answer looked positive is ordinary management, not evidence of dependence. The paper says controls 'seek access', which shows interest, not inability to work without the tool.
Paradis's lack of reported non-compliance may mean nobody checked. The control was an instruction to disable features, and the sections read describe no verification.
Shen and Tamkin's pilot non-compliance is about paid crowd workers taking a shortcut on a timed task, a different thing from professional developers refusing unassisted work.
METR's selection could be driven partly by the pay cut and by the task-level design, which lets developers see and avoid the no-AI draw. METR says so itself.
Fixed-task trials avoid the problem partly because participants cannot choose which work enters the study, not because developers are happy to work without AI.
verification_status: VERIFIED against the opened primary source: every Peng figure, date and design detail (arXiv PDF v1).

VERIFIED against the opened February 2025 MIT draft: Cui's 26.08% (SE 10.3%), 4,867 developers, per-firm sample sizes, randomisation units, dates, the Microsoft control-group statement, footnotes 3 and 8, adoption figures, the abandoned Accenture experiment.

VERIFIED via the Crossref record only: Management Science publication date (27 Feb 2026) and final abstract. The published article text itself was not opened (403), so any change to the body between draft and final is unchecked.
VERIFIED against arXiv v3: all Paradis figures, dates, design and limitations.
VERIFIED against the METR post's page text: every METR quote and figure listed here.
VERIFIED against the arXiv PDFs: Shen and Tamkin's 17%, n = 52, pilot non-compliance; Murphy-Hill's 24.0%, dates, synthetic-control design.

NOT VERIFIED: AEA registry entry AEARCTR-0014530 (server error; the draft itself says the trial was post-registered). SSRN dates. Paradis's ICSE-SEIP 2025 publication (seen only in Murphy-Hill's reference list).
NOT ESTABLISHED: that no other randomised developer-productivity trial was reported in 2026. Three web searches found none beyond METR's update, which is an absence of search results, not proof.
relevance_to_essay: Direct. Of the randomised trials checked, the two that needed a no-AI control to hold for months inside developers' own work both report losing it: Microsoft's control group sought access and the trial ended (May 2023), and METR's developers avoided the no-AI condition (2025 to 2026). The short fixed-task trials (Peng, Google, Shen and Tamkin) kept theirs. So the accurate claim is narrower than 'the control group is gone': long, real-work controls are failing, and one-sitting lab controls still work but need policing. Microsoft's own 2026 study of agentic tools dropped randomisation for a synthetic control.
implications_for_measurement: Short fixed-task experiments with a no-AI arm are still feasible, but compliance has to be verified (Shen and Tamkin needed screen recordings) and the result says little about real work.

Staggered rollout is the design firms can actually run: everyone gets the tool, the order is random, and early is compared with late (Cui's anonymous firm). The window is short and the estimate noisy (54% with a standard error of 43).

Expect imperfect compliance and plan the analysis for it. Cui's 26% is an effect on those who took the tool up, estimated with assignment as an instrument, because many treated developers did not use it and controls later did.

Where randomisation is not possible, the fallback seen in 2026 is observational: never-users as a synthetic control, with a placebo test (Murphy-Hill). The authors state the self-selection risk plainly.
A leader cannot cite a current randomised number for agentic tools in ordinary company work. The randomised evidence with a clean control is from 2022 to 2024 and from autocomplete-era tools.
open_questions: Whether the Management Science final text changed any design description from the February 2025 draft. Whether Google verified that control participants kept AI features off. How many completers Peng had in each arm. Whether any other randomised developer-productivity trial with a no-AI control reported results in 2026. Whether Microsoft's control group 'seeking access' reflected developer demand or a management decision; the paper gives one sentence and no counts.
